To forewarn someone means to warn them about something before it happens — especially something unpleasant, dangerous, or difficult — so that they have enough time to prepare, protect themselves, or simply not be caught off guard.

Think of it in two parts: "fore" (meaning before, in advance) + "warn" (to alert someone about danger or a problem). Put them together and you get: to alert someone ahead of time.
How It Feels in Real Life

Imagine your friend is about to meet your uncle, who is known for talking non-stop. Before they meet, you pull your friend aside and say, "I'm warning you — my uncle never stops talking." That right there is forewarning. You gave your friend a heads-up before the situation arrived, so they could mentally prepare.

Now imagine your friend meets your uncle with no such heads-up and is completely shocked. That's a situation where forewarning didn't happen.

The soul of this word is the time gap — the warning comes before the event, not during it or after.

These two words are close cousins, but not identical.

"Warn" simply means to tell someone about a danger or problem. The timing is flexible — it could happen right as the danger is unfolding, or just before.

"Forewarn" adds a clear emphasis: the warning happens well in advance, giving the person meaningful time to act on it. There is always a time gap between the warning and the event.

So every forewarning is a warning, but not every warning is a forewarning.

A lifeguard who shouts "Watch out! That wave is crashing on you NOW!" is warning you.
A lifeguard who tells you "The waves get dangerous around 4 PM — be careful if you're still in the water then" is forewarning you.

The person (or thing) that forewarns is someone who already knows about an upcoming event or risk — and chooses to pass that knowledge on to someone who doesn't know yet. The motive is almost always protective or helpful.

It can be:

  • A person (a doctor, a friend, a teacher, a government official)
  • An organization (a weather agency, a news channel)
  • A system or sign (an alarm, a notice, a label)

The doctor forewarned her patient that the new medication might cause dizziness.
The government forewarned citizens about the approaching storm.
A sign on the road forewarns drivers of a sharp bend ahead.
How to Use It in a Sentence

Forewarn + someone + about/of + something:

She forewarned her colleagues about the client's aggressive negotiating style.
The captain forewarned the crew of rough seas ahead.

Forewarn + someone + that + [full sentence]:

My manager forewarned me that the meeting would run very long.
They forewarned us that parking in that area was nearly impossible.

• It does not mean to threaten. A threat is meant to intimidate or scare. A forewarning is meant to help or protect.
  • It does not mean to predict. You can predict something privately in your head without telling anyone. To forewarn, you must communicate the warning to someone else.
  • It does not imply certainty. You can forewarn someone about something that might happen, not just something that will definitely happen. ("I'm forewarning you — this road might be flooded.")

• Forewarned (past tense): The residents were forewarned about the flood.
  • Forewarning (used as a noun or a continuous action): Without any forewarning, the power went out. / He kept forewarning everyone about the risks.
  • Forewarns (present tense, third person): This label forewarns users of potential side effects.
A Famous Phrase You Should Know

"Forewarned is forearmed."

This is one of the most well-known phrases in the English language. It means: if you know about a danger or difficulty in advance, you are already in a stronger position to face it. Knowledge ahead of time is itself a form of power and protection. This phrase perfectly captures the entire spirit of the word forewarn.

"Forewarn" is a word that sits on the slightly formal side of everyday English. You'll hear it in news reports, official communications, medical advice, and careful, serious conversation. You can use it casually with friends, and it will be perfectly understood — it just carries a slightly more serious, considered tone compared to simply saying "I'm giving you a heads-up."
The Complete Picture in One Sentence

To forewarn is to tell someone in advance about a coming danger, difficulty, or unpleasant situation, giving them the chance to prepare — and the defining quality of this word is always that advance nature: the warning arrives before the event does.
